title: Walk in Their Shoes
description: You spend four rounds as a customer service rep at Solara Telecom — handling frustrated customers, navigating policy, and managing your own exhaustion. Then you play the same four interactions again, this time as the customer on the other end of the line. The same decision looks completely different depending on which side of the phone you are on.
learning_concept: Empathy is not a feeling — it is a cognitive act of perspective-shifting. This game forces it by making you live the same interaction twice, from opposite sides, and then asking: does knowing what the rep was going through change what you feel about how they treated you?
learning_objectives: Develop perspective-taking as a deliberate practice, not just an emotional response
Understand how systemic pressures — policies, scripts, quotas, exhaustion — shape individual behavior
Recognize how the same interaction feels radically different depending on your role, power, and information
Build the skill of holding your own experience and another person's experience simultaneously without dismissing either

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: In Act 1 (rounds 1–4), you are Maya Chen, a customer service rep at Solara Telecom. You handle four customer calls with limited tools, constrained policy, and your own fatigue.
After round 4, the game transitions: 'You have seen this from the inside. Now let's go to the other side of the phone.'
In Act 2 (rounds 5–8), you replay the same four interactions — but now you are the customer who called in. You experience exactly what the rep did to you.
Rounds 5–8 include a reflection prompt after each choice: how does knowing what the rep was going through change what you feel?
Track three resources: Customer Satisfaction (how callers feel), Rep Wellbeing (how you are holding up as Maya), and Interaction Quality (the overall quality of the exchange).
tips: In Act 1, notice which choices feel right in the moment but might feel wrong from the other side.
In Act 2, try to remember exactly what the rep (you) was dealing with before judging their response.
Empathy is not about excusing poor treatment — it is about understanding what produced it.
The reflection prompts in Act 2 are the heart of the game. Take them seriously.

psychological_framework.description: This game is built on the difference between affective empathy (feeling what someone else feels) and cognitive empathy (understanding how they arrived at their experience). The role-reversal mechanic forces cognitive empathy by giving you information — the rep's pressures, constraints, and inner state — that you would not normally have as a customer. The central question the game asks: would you judge the rep differently if you knew what they knew?

core_skills.name: Empathy
core_skills.description: The ability to understand another person's experience from the inside — not just to feel sympathy for them, but to see the world through their constraints and pressures.

core_skills.name: Adaptability
core_skills.description: Shifting your frame of reference when new information becomes available — including information that challenges your initial judgment of someone.

core_skills.name: Resilience
core_skills.description: Sustaining professionalism and care under conditions of emotional labor, repetitive stress, and systemic constraint — the daily challenge of customer-facing work.

glossary_terms.definition: The work of managing your feelings and expressions to fulfill the emotional requirements of a job — typically in service work where you must appear calm, helpful, and positive regardless of how you feel.
glossary_terms.example: A call center rep who has just been screamed at by one customer must answer the next call with a warm, fresh greeting.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Sociologist Arlie Hochschild coined the term in 1983. Emotional labor has a real cost: it depletes the same psychological resources as physical labor. Workers who perform it continuously without recovery are at high risk of burnout, depersonalization, and disengagement.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Airlines train flight attendants to manage passenger anxiety during turbulence with reassuring calm — even when the flight attendant is themselves scared. That managed performance is emotional labor.

glossary_terms.definition: The tendency to explain other people's behavior through their character rather than their circumstances, while explaining our own behavior through our circumstances.
glossary_terms.example: When a rep is abrupt, we think 'they are rude.' When we are abrupt, we think 'I am having a terrible day.'
glossary_terms.deep_dive: This cognitive bias is one of the most robust findings in social psychology. We consistently overweight character and underweight context when judging others. The role-reversal mechanic in this game directly targets this bias by giving you access to the context you would normally not have.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Research by Lee Ross at Stanford showed that when people learned about situational constraints on a person's behavior, their judgments of that person's character softened significantly — but only when the information was made salient.

glossary_terms.definition: The deliberate cognitive act of imagining a situation from another person's point of view — including their information, their constraints, their goals, and their emotional state.
glossary_terms.example: Before sending a frustrated email to a colleague, pausing to ask: 'What are they likely dealing with that I cannot see?'
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Perspective-taking is different from perspective-seeking (actually asking someone about their experience). It is a solo practice you can do at any time. Research by Adam Galinsky at Columbia shows it improves negotiation outcomes, reduces bias, and increases the quality of collaborative decisions.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Doctors who are trained in perspective-taking protocols have patients who report higher satisfaction and are more likely to follow treatment recommendations — not because the doctors changed their medical approach, but because they changed how they communicated.

halftime_config.reflection_question: You have just completed your shift as Maya. Before you become the customer: what was the hardest part of her job? What did the callers not know about what she was dealing with?
halftime_config.custom_message: You have seen this from the inside. Now let's go to the other side of the phone.

rounds.title: Act 1 — The Billing Dispute [As Rep]
rounds.story:
You are Maya Chen, six hours into an eight-hour shift at Solara Telecom's customer service center. Your headset is cutting in and out on your left ear and you reported it three days ago — still no replacement. Your metrics are tracked in real time on a screen above you: average handle time, customer satisfaction score, first-call resolution rate. Your supervisor reminded you this morning that your handle time is running 22 seconds above target.

The next call connects. A man named David Reyes is calling about a billing error — his plan was quietly upgraded without his consent and his bill is $47 higher than it should be. He is firm but not yet hostile. He wants a refund. Company policy allows you to issue a one-time courtesy credit up to $30 without manager approval. A full $47 refund requires escalation, which will almost certainly push your handle time over target and may affect your weekly score. Your supervisor is watching from across the floor.

You have thirty seconds before the silence becomes awkward. What do you do?
rounds.goal: Handle David's billing dispute as Maya the rep
rounds.coaching_moment: Notice the gap between what you know is right for the customer and what the system makes easy for you. That gap is where emotional labor lives — and where many service failures are born.

choices.label: Issue the $30 credit immediately and explain the escalation process for the remaining $17
choices.feedback: David is mildly satisfied but not happy. He appreciates that you acted immediately on what you could, but the $17 remaining feels like bureaucratic friction he should not have to navigate. You handled the call with calm transparency and took the action within your authority — a solid if imperfect outcome. Your handle time came in just over target. Your supervisor makes a note.

choices.label: Escalate the full $47 refund — David deserves the correct outcome even if it costs you your handle time
choices.feedback: David gets the full refund. He thanks you sincerely and the call ends on a genuinely warm note. But the escalation took eleven extra minutes and blew your handle time metrics for the day. Your supervisor calls you aside at break and says your numbers are 'a concern.' You did the right thing for the customer. The system has registered it as underperformance. This tension — between doing right by the customer and surviving the metrics — is the invisible war of service work.
choices.coaching_moment: Doing right by the customer sometimes costs the rep something real. This is not a hypothetical — it is the daily reality of service work under metric surveillance.

choices.label: Offer only the $30 credit and close the call quickly — protect your handle time
choices.feedback: David is left with an unresolved problem. He agreed to the $30 credit only because he was tired of arguing, not because he was satisfied. Your metrics look clean. But David is already composing a negative review in his head. More importantly, you know you did not give him what he deserved. That knowledge sits with you for the rest of the shift in a way that is hard to name but easy to feel.

rounds.reflection_prompt: Before switching sides, what assumptions were you making about the other person's experience?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Act 1 — The Technical Failure [As Rep]
rounds.story:
The next call is a woman named Sandra Park. She has been without internet for four days. She works from home — she had to go to a cafe to make this call on her mobile data. Her voice has the specific exhaustion of someone who has been transferred three times already and told to 'wait for a technician' twice without anyone ever arriving.

You check her account. The issue is on your side — a network configuration problem in her neighborhood that was flagged two days ago and is apparently being worked on. The estimated fix time in the system is listed as 'TBD.' You are not authorized to promise a specific resolution date. You are authorized to offer a service credit for the outage days.

Sandra says: 'I do not want a credit. I want to know when it will be fixed.' You do not know. You genuinely do not know. And you cannot pretend you do.
rounds.goal: Handle Sandra's internet outage call honestly under uncertainty
rounds.coaching_moment: Honesty under uncertainty is one of the hardest things in service work. Scripts push you toward vague reassurance. But vague reassurance is the thing that erodes trust the fastest.

choices.label: Tell Sandra honestly that you do not know the timeline and explain why, then offer the service credit
choices.feedback: Sandra is quiet for a moment. Then she says: 'I appreciate you not pretending.' She is still frustrated, but something in her frustration shifts. She is no longer fighting the system — she is having a conversation with a person. You give her your direct callback extension and promise to check the status again at end of day. You do not know if the issue will be fixed. But you have made a human connection out of an impersonal failure, and that matters more than she will likely say.

choices.label: Give Sandra a vague reassurance — 'It should be resolved soon' — and move on
choices.feedback: 'Soon' means nothing. Sandra has heard 'soon' three times from three different people. The call ends neutrally but she calls back two hours later, angrier than before, and gets a different rep who has to start from scratch. You protected yourself from a hard conversation and created a worse outcome for everyone. The instinct to soothe with vagueness is understandable — it is just almost always wrong.

choices.label: Escalate to a supervisor and ask them to make a commitment Sandra can hold someone accountable to
choices.feedback: You put Sandra on hold and walk over to your supervisor. She is not pleased about the interruption but she makes the call — she pulls the technical ticket and promises Sandra a 48-hour resolution window with a callback from a senior technician. Sandra accepts. Your supervisor marks this as an appropriate escalation. More importantly, Sandra got a real answer. The system worked, but only because you pushed it.

rounds.reflection_prompt: When a technical failure is not your fault, how do you still own the customer's experience of it?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Act 1 — The Angry Caller [As Rep]
rounds.story:
The call quality is fine. The problem is the person. Marcus Webb has been a Solara customer for eleven years and he is furious — not the sharp, specific fury of someone with a grievance, but the wide, exhausted fury of someone who has been failed by institutions repeatedly and is now putting years of that frustration into this call. He uses profanity in his third sentence. He calls the company 'incompetent garbage.' He has not yet explained his actual problem.

You are seven hours into your shift. Your ear is still hurting from the faulty headset. Your satisfaction score took a hit from an earlier call where the system logged the customer as 'dissatisfied' even though the issue was resolved. You have fifteen minutes until your break.

You know from training that you are permitted to issue one verbal warning and then terminate a call if the caller becomes abusive. You also know that Marcus's account shows he has never called before and his issue — once you pull it up — is a legitimate one.
rounds.goal: Navigate Marcus's call while protecting your own wellbeing
rounds.coaching_moment: De-escalation is a skill that requires energy reserves. When you are depleted, it is harder to regulate your own reaction before you can calm someone else's. This is the invisible cost of emotional labor stacking up across a shift.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Right now, as Maya: what would you need in order to genuinely help Marcus instead of just managing him? What is getting in the way of that?

choices.label: Name what you are hearing before addressing the issue: 'I can hear how frustrated you are. Let me help.'
choices.feedback: Marcus stops mid-sentence. Something shifts. He says: 'Yeah. Sorry. It's been — yes.' You pull up his issue — a legitimate billing error — and solve it in six minutes. The call ends with Marcus saying he has 'actually never had a good call with customer service before.' You hang up tired but not depleted. Validation before solution is a technique that feels counterintuitive under time pressure. It is also the fastest path through an emotional call.
choices.coaching_moment: The instinct under pressure is to solve the problem immediately. But when someone is emotionally flooded, they cannot process solutions until they feel heard. Acknowledgment is not a delay — it is a prerequisite.

choices.label: Issue the verbal warning about profanity immediately and make the policy clear
choices.feedback: Marcus quiets down — he does not want to get disconnected. But the dynamic has shifted into compliance rather than resolution. He gives you the minimum information, you process the minimum fix, and the call ends in cold silence. He does not feel helped. You feel vaguely hollow about it. Policy was followed. The human exchange was not.

choices.label: Transfer Marcus to a colleague — you are too depleted to handle this well right now
choices.feedback: You pass the call to Daria, a colleague who joined the shift two hours ago and has fresh energy. Marcus eventually gets helped. You sit quietly for two minutes before your next call, recovering enough to be present again. Knowing your own limits and acting on them is not weakness — it is a professional judgment. The question is whether the system gives you enough space to make that call without it counting against you. Spoiler: often it doesn't.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Act 1 — The Loyal Customer Leaving [As Rep]
rounds.story:
Your final call before break is Linda Vasquez. She is polite, even apologetic. She has been a Solara customer for nine years and she wants to cancel. She has found a better plan with a competitor — the same speeds, twenty dollars less per month. She is not angry. She is just done.

You have been trained in a 'save' script — a series of offers designed to retain customers on the verge of canceling. You can offer a loyalty discount of up to $15 per month. You could also just process the cancellation smoothly, thank her for nine years of loyalty, and let her go with her dignity intact.

The retention script works — it saves about 30% of customers who are called. But Linda sounds decided. And you are tired.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle Linda's cancellation request
rounds.coaching_moment: Sometimes the most respectful thing you can do for a long-term customer is let them leave well. Retention scripts save numbers. Genuine respect for a customer's decision builds the kind of loyalty that might actually bring them back.

choices.label: Run the retention script — offer the $15 loyalty discount and see if she stays
choices.feedback: Linda accepts the discount and stays. Your retention metric gets a tick. But the conversation felt like a transaction — you offered the script, she accepted the number. There was no acknowledgment of nine years. No 'thank you for being with us this long.' She is still a customer, but the relationship has been reduced to a price point. You have kept her for now. Whether she tells anyone good things about Solara is another question.

choices.label: Offer the loyalty discount but acknowledge the nine years first — genuinely
choices.feedback: You say: 'Linda, nine years is a long time to trust a company with something as essential as your internet. I want to say that first.' There is a pause. She says: 'Thank you. That is kind.' You offer the discount. She accepts. But more than the discount, the acknowledgment of her loyalty catches her off guard in the best way. She tells a friend about the call the next day — not because of the discount, but because of the four seconds you spent actually seeing her.
choices.coaching_moment: Acknowledgment before transaction costs nothing. It is the difference between a customer who stays because of a price point and one who stays because they feel seen.

choices.label: Process the cancellation cleanly and thank her for nine years without the script
choices.feedback: You skip the script and say: 'I can process that for you. And I want to say — nine years is a long time, and we appreciate that. I am sorry we could not find a way to keep you.' Linda is surprised by the directness and warmth. The call is the shortest of your day and one of the most satisfying. Linda hangs up thinking: 'That rep was actually decent.' She tells her husband about it that evening.

rounds.reflection_prompt: A loyal customer leaving is different from an angry one. What does loyalty require from the company's side?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Act 2 — The Billing Dispute [As Customer]
rounds.story:
You are now David Reyes. You have discovered a $47 charge on your Solara bill for a plan upgrade you did not request. You are not the kind of person who complains easily — this is only the second time you have ever called a company to dispute a charge. You are a little nervous, actually, about seeming difficult.

The rep who answers sounds a little flat — not rude, but clearly running a routine. She tells you she can issue a $30 credit immediately but a full refund requires escalation. The way she says 'escalation' sounds like 'problem.' You sense she is trying to close this call.

You now know something the David of round 1 did not: that rep has a handle time target, a supervisor watching her, and a broken headset that has been hurting her ear for three days. Does that change what you do next?
rounds.goal: Respond to the rep's offer as David, the customer
rounds.coaching_moment: The customer who knows what the rep is dealing with is the customer who can make a different choice. This is what empathy looks like when it is given information to work with.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How did this choice feel when you were the rep in round 1? Does knowing what Maya was dealing with change anything about how you feel being on this side of it?

choices.label: Accept the $30 credit — the rep seems under pressure and you can escalate in writing later
choices.feedback: You take the $30 and end the call politely. The rep sounds genuinely relieved. You feel mild residual frustration about the $17 — not enough to ruin your day, just enough to notice. You email the billing dispute team that evening and get the remaining credit within 48 hours without another phone call. Knowing what the rep was dealing with made you more patient. Patience had a cost — seventeen dollars and fifteen minutes of your evening. It also had a value you cannot fully measure.

choices.label: Politely but firmly ask for the full refund — the billing error was the company's fault, not yours
choices.feedback: You hold your ground without being unkind. You say: 'I understand there is a process, but I was charged for something I did not request. Can we get the full amount corrected today?' The rep escalates. She sounds tired when she puts you on hold. The refund comes through eleven minutes later. You got what you deserved. The rep's metrics took a hit. Both things are true simultaneously. Sometimes asserting your rights has a cost for the person in front of you that you cannot fully see.

choices.label: Ask the rep how she is doing before making any demands — you notice something in her voice
choices.feedback: You say: 'Before we sort this out — it sounds like it has been a long day. I am not in a rush.' There is a pause. The rep says: 'That is... kind of you to say.' The conversation that follows is the most human interaction either of you will have in a Solara context today. She credits you the full $47 within three minutes, which she technically was not authorized to do but which felt entirely right. You both hang up lighter than when you started.
choices.coaching_moment: The most powerful thing you can do for someone who is performing emotional labor is to momentarily release them from the performance. One genuine acknowledgment can change the entire structure of an interaction.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Act 2 — The Technical Failure [As Customer]
rounds.story:
You are Sandra Park. You have been without internet for four days. You work from home and had to take this call from the parking lot of a coffee shop, on your mobile data, with your laptop balanced on the passenger seat. You have called twice before and been told 'soon' both times.

The rep who answers this time sounds different from the previous two. She is calm, direct. She tells you she does not know the exact timeline — something in the system says 'TBD' — but she explains why: the issue is a neighborhood configuration problem that their network team is actively working on. She offers you a service credit for the outage days.

You now know what you did not know as Sandra in round 2: the rep genuinely does not have access to the technical team's schedule. The 'TBD' is not a dodge — it is the actual information available to her. The previous reps who said 'soon' were either guessing or lying. This one is telling you the truth.
rounds.goal: Respond to the rep's honest answer as Sandra
rounds.coaching_moment: Honesty without certainty is a rare gift in service interactions. The question is whether you can recognize it when you are the one who is frustrated and needs an answer.
rounds.reflection_prompt: In round 2, how did it feel to not know the answer and have to say so? Now that you are Sandra — does knowing the rep was being honest rather than evasive change how you want to respond?

choices.label: Accept the honest answer and the service credit — and thank her for not giving you vague reassurance
choices.feedback: You say: 'You are the first person who has not told me it will be fixed soon. Thank you for that.' There is a pause. Then the rep says: 'I know it is hard not having a timeline. I am sorry I cannot give you one.' The credit is small. The honest exchange is not. You hang up still frustrated — you still have no internet — but you feel like you were treated like an adult instead of a problem to be managed.

choices.label: Push for a committed resolution date — honest or not, you need something to hold the company to
choices.feedback: The rep escalates to her supervisor, who commits to a 48-hour window. You have a real deadline now. The rep did the right thing by escalating. But you notice she sounded anxious when she put you on hold — like she was worried about the escalation counting against her. Your need for certainty is completely legitimate. Getting it had a cost for her that you can now partly see.

choices.label: Lose patience — four days is four days, and honesty does not fix the problem
choices.feedback: Your frustration overwhelms your appreciation for the honest answer. You escalate your tone. The rep — who was genuinely doing her best — shifts from empathetic to defensive. The information exchange stops and the call becomes about managing you. You hang up angrier than before. Your frustration was completely understandable. But directing it at the one rep who was actually being honest with you was the one move that made the situation worse.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Act 2 — The Angry Caller [As Customer]
rounds.story:
You are Marcus Webb. Eleven years with Solara. Your most recent bill has a charge for a roaming package you used once in January — you were told it would be removed after one month. It is now March and it is still there. You have called twice about this. Both times someone said it was 'taken care of.' It is not taken care of.

You are aware, in this moment, that your frustration is bigger than $24.99. You are aware that it is about trust and about feeling dismissed. You are also aware — because you have now stood on the other side of this call — that the person who picks up your call today is not responsible for the two previous reps who failed you. They are a person, seven hours into a shift, with a broken headset probably, trying to manage a system that does not give them what they need.

You still need the problem solved. But you now have information you did not have before.
rounds.goal: Handle your own frustration on this call, knowing what you know now
rounds.coaching_moment: Knowing what is happening on the other side of the line does not make your frustration illegitimate. It does give you a choice about what to do with it.
rounds.reflection_prompt: In round 3, what did it feel like to receive a call from Marcus in the state he was in? Now that you are Marcus — what do you actually want to do with that knowledge?

choices.label: Name your frustration clearly but direct it at the company's process, not the rep
choices.feedback: You open with: 'I want to be clear upfront — my frustration is not with you. It is with a process that failed me twice. I would like your help to fix it.' The rep exhales audibly. She resolves the issue in four minutes. She thanks you at the end — genuinely. You hang up knowing that you were still the customer and you still got what you needed, but you did not take it out on the person in front of you. That distinction matters more than the $24.99.
choices.coaching_moment: Directing frustration at the system rather than the person is an act of cognitive empathy in real time. It requires holding two things simultaneously: your legitimate anger and someone else's innocence.

choices.label: Start from scratch as if you are calling for the first time — calm, factual, patient
choices.feedback: You suppress the accumulated frustration and give the rep a clean slate. The issue gets resolved efficiently. You feel a controlled sense of pride at having managed yourself well. The rep sounds genuinely appreciative of a caller who knows what they need and asks for it directly. You did not get to express the frustration — which means it is still in there. But the interaction was clean and the outcome was good.

choices.label: Let the frustration out — you know what the rep is dealing with, but you still need to be heard
choices.feedback: You cannot hold it. The eleven years, the two broken promises, the $24.99 — it all comes out. The rep stays professional but becomes distant. She solves the problem but the warmth is gone. Afterwards, you sit with a complicated feeling: your anger was real, your history was real, and you still made someone's seven-hour shift harder for reasons that were not their fault. Sometimes empathy arrives as guilt after the fact. That matters too.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Act 2 — The Loyal Customer Leaving [As Customer]
rounds.story:
You are Linda Vasquez. Nine years with Solara. The new plan from GigaNet is $20 cheaper per month for the same speed. You are not doing this out of anger — you just want the better price. It is sensible. You feel slightly guilty about it, which is its own interesting thing.

The rep who answers is clearly tired. But she says something to you before the script: 'Nine years is a long time to trust a company with something as essential as your internet. I want to say that first.' You were not expecting that. It is a small thing and a large thing at the same time.

She then offers you a $15 monthly loyalty discount. With the discount, Solara is now only $5 more per month than GigaNet. You now have to decide whether the thing she said — the acknowledgment — changes the math.
rounds.goal: Decide whether to stay or leave as Linda
rounds.coaching_moment: Price is rational. Loyalty is emotional. This round asks: what is genuine acknowledgment actually worth to you? Not in principle — in this moment, with this decision, with $60 a year on the line.
rounds.reflection_prompt: In round 4, which option did you choose as Maya? Do you wish the rep who handled your call as Linda had made the same choice? Does what you did then change what you want to do now?

choices.label: Stay with Solara — the acknowledgment mattered and $5 a month is worth the continuity
choices.feedback: You tell her you will stay. She sounds surprised and genuinely pleased. You hang up having made a choice that is not fully rational — $5 per month is still $60 per year — but that feels right in a way that is hard to articulate. What you actually paid for was a moment of being seen by an institution that usually does not see you. Whether that is worth $60 a year is a question only you can answer. But you answered it. And you do not regret it.

choices.label: Leave anyway — the acknowledgment was nice but $60 a year is $60 a year
choices.feedback: You thank her sincerely for what she said — you mean it — and you process the cancellation. She takes it professionally and with genuine warmth. You hang up with the unusual feeling of having had a good interaction with a company you are leaving. The acknowledgment did not change the math, but it changed how you feel about the company. There is a non-zero chance you come back in two years. That is worth something Solara will never be able to measure.

choices.label: Ask for a bigger discount — the acknowledgment was meaningful but you still want a better deal
choices.feedback: You say: 'I appreciate that genuinely. Is there any chance the discount could go higher?' The rep pauses and says she is not authorized above $15. You thank her and process the cancellation anyway. A small moment of commerce overriding connection. Completely rational. The interaction was still better than most. You both knew it.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Replaying the same four interactions from opposite perspectives
transfer_exercises.real_world: Think of a recent conflict or frustrating interaction you had. Write a one-paragraph account of the same interaction from the other person's perspective — including what pressures they might have been under that you could not see.
transfer_exercises.challenge: Before your next difficult conversation, spend two minutes asking: what is the most charitable explanation for why this person behaved the way they did? Then lead with that assumption.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Sustaining professionalism as Maya across a long, draining shift
transfer_exercises.real_world: Map your own emotional labor this week: when are you performing a feeling you do not have? When does that performance feel sustainable, and when does it cost you? Identify one recovery practice you can build into draining days.
transfer_exercises.challenge: For one week, log one moment each day where you performed an emotion rather than felt it. At the end of the week, look at the patterns: what contexts trigger the most emotional labor? What helps you recover?

achievements.name: Full Circle
achievements.description: Completed all 8 rounds with both Act 1 and Act 2 choices landing in the empathy-positive zone — seeing both sides clearly and acting on what you saw.

achievements.name: The Other Side
achievements.description: In at least 3 Act 2 rounds, explicitly referenced what you learned in Act 1 to make a more empathetic choice as the customer.

achievements.name: Honest Mirror
achievements.description: In round 6 as Sandra, recognized and acknowledged the rep's honest answer rather than escalating — demonstrating that empathy can function even under personal frustration.

cultural_context: India is among the world's most climate-vulnerable nations. Environmental thinking is increasingly integrated into India's school curricula under NEP 2020, preparing students for the sustainability challenges of India's development.
coaching_moment: Understanding how others feel and think is the foundation of every great relationship and team.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Walk in Their Shoes Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 4 rounds of Walk in Their Shoes. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
